title: Phonological Awareness tasks for Italian-English comparison
author: Chiara Valeria Marinelli

steps_raw.instruction: Phonological Awareness tasks
An attempt was made to develop tasks that would be comparable between the Italian (i.e., a consistent orthography) and English (i.e., an inconsistent orthography)versions.

Phonological awareness was measured using a spoonerisms and a phoneme deletion task. Typically, there is a relatively narrow range of performance on phonological awareness tasks in readers of regular languages (e.g., Cossu et al., 1988) and this may limit their predictive power. For this reason, we used two tests (phoneme deletion and spoonerisms tasks) not susceptible to ceiling effect and sensitive to capture individual differences in older children and adults (Bruck, 1992; de Jong & van der Leij, 2003; Hatcher, Snowling & Griffiths, 2002; Hulme et al., 2002; Landerl et al., 1997; Paulesu et al., 2001; Ramus et al., 2003), as well as in very young children (Caravolas et al., 2005).

The child was read aloud 24 pairs of words and asked to exchange the first sounds of the two words and say aloud the resulting words (for example, pala-sera generated sala-pera when the first sounds were exchanged). Twelve pairs resulted in real words and twelve did not. In the scoring, one point was awarded for each correct pair, ½ a point if only one of the words of the pair was correct. Self-corrections were counted as errors.

“I’m going to read you words. Listen carefully, as your task is to exchange the first sounds of the words and say aloud the result. Do not think about the way words are spelled, only think of the sounds. I will tell you whether you should obtain new words or made-up words.”
Phoneme-deletion task

The child was given a spoken by-syllabic word and one of its phonemes. He was asked to repeat the word without the presented phoneme. For example; “repeat ‘table’ without /t/”. The task had forty trials. Twenty resulted in other real words and twenty in non-words after the phoneme deletion. For both sets, there were five items for each position to delete (from 1st to 4th position). Stimuli were presented in a quasi-random order. The child was encouraged to think to the sounds of words not its letters. One point was scored for each correct trial. Self-corrections were counted as errors.

“I am going to say a word and then one of its sounds. For example, I may say /table/ and then the sound /t/. You should listen carefully and then repeat the word back but without the sound. So if I said /table/ and /t/ you would say /able/. Taking away a sound may result in a real word like in the case of table without /t/ /able’ or in a made up word. For example, /cabbage/ without /c/ is /abbage/ which is not a real word. Do not think about the way the words are spelled, only think of the sounds.”
